tool.name: Next.js
tool.tagline: Full-stack React framework with file-based routing, Server Components and caching
tool.description: Next.js is the most widely used React framework: it adds file-system routing, server rendering, React Server Components, Server Actions, caching and built-in optimisations for images, fonts and metadata. With the App Router you build full-stack apps where data fetching and mutations live next to the components that use them. It deploys to Vercel, any Node.js server, containers or static hosting.

concepts.name: Creating a Next.js app
concepts.summary: Scaffold a project with create-next-app, run the dev server, and understand the files and folders it generates.
concepts.why: Knowing the default setup and project layout makes every later Next.js concept easier to place.
concepts.body:
Create a project with `npx create-next-app@latest my-app`. The recommended defaults give you TypeScript, ESLint, Tailwind CSS, the **App Router**, **Cache Components** (Next.js 16's caching model) and an `AGENTS.md` file for coding assistants, with the `@/*` import alias pointing at the project root.

Scripts in `package.json`:

- `next dev` — development server with Fast Refresh, using **Turbopack** (the default bundler since Next.js 16).
- `next build` — production build: compiles, prerenders what it can and reports each route.
- `next start` — runs the production server.

Key folders and files:

- `app/` — the App Router. Folders become URL segments; special files like `page.tsx` and `layout.tsx` define the UI. `app/layout.tsx` is the required **root layout** containing `<html>` and `<body>`.
- `public/` — static files served from `/` (e.g. `public/logo.svg` at `/logo.svg`).
- `next.config.ts` — framework configuration, typed with `NextConfig`.
- `.env*` files — environment variables.

There is also the older **Pages Router** (`pages/` directory). It is still supported, but new projects should use the App Router, which is what this curriculum covers.

Next.js runs on React 19 and makes **Server Components** the default: components in `app/` render on the server unless you opt into the client. Keep that in mind from day one.
takeaways: `create-next-app` defaults: TypeScript, Tailwind, ESLint, App Router, Turbopack, Cache Components
`app/` holds routes; `app/layout.tsx` is the required root layout with html and body
`next dev`, `next build`, `next start` are the core commands
pitfalls: Mixing tutorials for the Pages Router (`pages/`, `getServerSideProps`) with an App Router project.

quiz.q: Which file must exist at the top of the app directory and render <html> and <body>?
quiz.explain: The App Router requires a root layout that defines the html and body tags.

concepts.name: Pages, layouts and file-based routing
concepts.summary: Create routes with folders and page files, and share UI between them with nested layouts.
concepts.why: File-based routing is the backbone of every Next.js app; layouts avoid repeating navigation and shells.
concepts.body:
In the App Router, **folders define URL segments** and special files define what renders:

- `page.tsx` makes a segment publicly accessible and exports the page component. `app/page.tsx` is `/`, `app/blog/page.tsx` is `/blog`, `app/blog/archive/page.tsx` is `/blog/archive`.
- `layout.tsx` wraps all pages below it. It receives `children` (the page or nested layout) and is shared across navigations.

A folder without `page.tsx` is not a route, so you can **colocate** components, tests and styles inside `app/` safely. Prefix a folder with an underscore (`_components`) to make the intent explicit.

**Layouts nest**: `app/layout.tsx` wraps `app/dashboard/layout.tsx`, which wraps `app/dashboard/settings/page.tsx`. On navigation between pages under the same layout, the layout **is not re-rendered** and keeps its state: an open sidebar or a search input stays as it was. Only the changed segment renders. (If you need a fresh instance per navigation, use `template.tsx` instead of `layout.tsx`.)

Pages and layouts are Server Components by default and can be `async`.

Other special files you will meet soon: `loading.tsx`, `error.tsx`, `not-found.tsx` and `route.ts`. Next.js composes them into a fixed hierarchy per segment: layout, then template, error boundary, loading boundary, not-found boundary, and finally the page.
takeaways: Folders = URL segments; `page.tsx` makes a segment routable
`layout.tsx` wraps child segments and keeps its state across navigations
Files without `page.tsx` (or in `_folders`) can be colocated safely
pitfalls: Putting per-page data or state in a layout and expecting it to reset on navigation; layouts persist.

quiz.q: You navigate from /dashboard to /dashboard/settings. What happens to the dashboard layout?
options: It stays mounted and keeps its state; only the page segment changes
It re-runs but loses client state
quiz.explain: Layouts are preserved on navigation between their child routes.

concepts.name: Linking and navigation
concepts.summary: Navigate with <Link>, understand prefetching and client-side transitions, and navigate programmatically.
concepts.why: Fast navigation is a key Next.js benefit, and it depends on using Link and the navigation hooks correctly.
concepts.body:
Use the **`<Link>`** component from `next/link` for internal navigation: `<Link href="/blog">Blog</Link>`. It renders an `<a>` but performs a **client-side transition**: only the changed segments are fetched and rendered, layouts keep their state, and the browser doesn't reload.

**Prefetching**: in production, links are prefetched when they enter the viewport or are hovered, so the next page is often ready before the click. How much is prefetched depends on the route; with Next.js 16's Partial Prefetching, the static App Shell of a route is prefetched by default. Pass `prefetch={false}` to disable it for rarely used links.

In **Client Components**, the hooks from `next/navigation` give you programmatic control:

- `useRouter()` — `router.push('/path')`, `router.replace`, `router.back()`, `router.refresh()` (re-fetch server data for the current route).
- `usePathname()` — the current path, e.g. to highlight the active link.
- `useSearchParams()` — read query parameters.
- `useParams()` — dynamic route params.

On the **server** (Server Components, Server Actions, Route Handlers), call `redirect('/login')` from `next/navigation`. It throws a special error that the framework handles, so code after it doesn't run.

Plain `<a>` tags work but cause full page loads. External links can use `<a>` directly.
takeaways: `<Link>` does client-side transitions and prefetches in production
`useRouter`, `usePathname`, `useSearchParams` come from `next/navigation` (client only)
Use `redirect()` on the server; it throws and stops execution
pitfalls: Importing `useRouter` from `next/router` (Pages Router) in an App Router component; use `next/navigation`.

quiz.q: Why prefer <Link href="/blog"> over <a href="/blog"> for internal links?
options: a tags don't work in Next.js
Link performs a client-side transition with prefetching and preserved layouts instead of a full reload
quiz.explain: Link enables soft navigation and prefetching; a plain anchor reloads the whole document.

concepts.name: Dynamic routes, params and searchParams
concepts.summary: Create [slug] and catch-all segments, read params and searchParams as promises, and type them with PageProps.
concepts.why: Blogs, products and user pages are all dynamic routes; params handling changed in recent versions.
concepts.body:
Wrap a folder name in square brackets to create a **dynamic segment**: `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` matches `/blog/hello-world`.

- `[...slug]` is a **catch-all**: `/docs/a/b/c` gives `slug = ['a', 'b', 'c']`.
- `[[...slug]]` is an **optional catch-all** that also matches `/docs`.

Pages receive **`params`** and **`searchParams`** props, and both are **Promises** (since Next.js 15). Await them in an async Server Component:

```tsx
export default async function Page({ params }: PageProps<'/blog/[slug]'>) {
  const { slug } = await params
}
```

`PageProps<'/route'>` and `LayoutProps<'/route'>` are **global type helpers** generated from your routes (by `next dev`, `next build` or `next typegen`), so params are typed without manual annotations. Layouts receive `params` but not `searchParams`.

In Client Components, read the promise with React's `use(params)`, or use the `useParams()` and `useSearchParams()` hooks.

Params are always strings (or string arrays for catch-alls); convert and validate them yourself. Call `notFound()` when the slug doesn't exist.

Values of dynamic params are only known at request time unless you list them with **`generateStaticParams`**, which lets Next.js prerender those pages at build time. You will use it when you learn about prerendering.
takeaways: `[slug]`, `[...slug]`, `[[...slug]]` create dynamic segments
`params` and `searchParams` are Promises: await them (or `use()` in client code)
`PageProps<'/route'>` types them automatically
pitfalls: Accessing `params.slug` without awaiting; in Next.js 15+ params is a Promise.

quiz.q: For the file app/docs/[...slug]/page.tsx, what is the awaited params.slug for /docs/guides/intro?
quiz.explain: Catch-all segments produce an array of the matched path segments.

concepts.name: Server and Client Components
concepts.summary: Know what runs where: Server Components by default, 'use client' boundaries for interactivity, and the rules for props across the boundary.
concepts.why: Every architectural decision in an App Router app follows from where each component runs.
concepts.body:
In the App Router every component is a **Server Component** unless marked otherwise. Server Components:

- run on the server (at build time or per request) and send **no JavaScript** for themselves to the browser,
- can be `async` and access databases, files and secrets directly,
- cannot use state, effects, event handlers or browser APIs.

For interactivity, create a **Client Component** by putting `'use client'` at the top of a file. That file and everything it imports become part of the client bundle. Client Components are still pre-rendered to HTML on the server and then **hydrated** in the browser.

Composition rules:

- Server Components can import and render Client Components, passing **serialisable props** (strings, numbers, plain objects, arrays, Dates, Promises, JSX, Server Actions), but not ordinary functions or class instances.
- Client Components cannot import Server Components, but can receive them as `children` or other JSX props. This is how you wrap server-rendered content in a client provider or modal.
- Push `'use client'` to the **leaves**: make the button interactive, not the whole page, to keep bundles small.
- Context providers are Client Components; render them in a layout and pass the rest of the tree as `children`.

Mark modules that must never reach the browser with `import 'server-only'`; the build fails if a Client Component imports them.
takeaways: Components are Server Components by default: async, server-only, no client JS
`'use client'` marks a boundary; props crossing it must be serialisable
Pass Server Components into Client Components as children; keep client islands small
pitfalls: Adding `'use client'` to a page or layout, turning its whole subtree into client code.

quiz.q: A Server Component wants to give a Client Component an onClick handler defined in the server file. What happens?
options: It runs on the server when clicked
It fails: ordinary functions are not serialisable across the boundary (only Server Actions can be passed)
Next.js converts it into a Route Handler
quiz.explain: Only serialisable values and Server Functions can be passed from server to client components.

concepts.name: Fetching data in Server Components
concepts.summary: Load data with async Server Components using fetch or a database, avoid waterfalls, and dedupe with React cache.
concepts.why: Server-side data fetching is the default and most efficient way to load data in an App Router app.
concepts.body:
In the App Router you fetch data where you need it: make a Server Component `async` and `await` the data, from `fetch`, an ORM or a database client.

```tsx
export default async function Page() {
  const posts = await db.post.findMany()
  return <PostList posts={posts} />
}
```

No `useEffect`, no loading flags, no API route in between, and secrets stay on the server.

Things to know:

- `fetch` results are **not cached by default**; uncached data is fetched at request time. Caching is opt-in with `'use cache'` (covered later).
- Identical `fetch` calls in one render are **memoised**, so several components can request the same URL without duplicate requests. For database calls, wrap the function with React's `cache()` to get the same per-request deduplication.
- Sequential `await`s create **waterfalls**. Start independent requests together with `Promise.all`, or let separate components fetch their own data inside separate Suspense boundaries so they stream in parallel.
- Handle failures: check `res.ok`, and decide between rendering a message, `notFound()` or throwing to an error boundary.

Client-side fetching is still useful for data that changes after load or depends on client state; use a library like SWR or TanStack Query, or pass a promise from a Server Component and read it with `use()`.
takeaways: Make Server Components async and await data directly
fetch is uncached by default; identical fetches in a render are memoised
Use `Promise.all` or separate Suspense boundaries to avoid waterfalls; `cache()` dedupes DB calls
pitfalls: Awaiting independent requests one after another, so the page takes the sum of their durations.

quiz.q: Two independent requests take 300 ms and 500 ms. They are awaited sequentially in a Server Component. Roughly how long until the page can render?
quiz.explain: Sequential awaits add up; Promise.all would bring it to about 500 ms.

concepts.name: Styling: global CSS, CSS Modules and Tailwind
concepts.summary: Style a Next.js app with global stylesheets, locally scoped CSS Modules and Tailwind CSS.
concepts.why: Every app needs styles, and Next.js supports several approaches with specific rules about where they can be imported.
concepts.body:
Next.js supports several styling approaches out of the box.

**Tailwind CSS** is set up by default in new projects. Tailwind v4 needs only `@import "tailwindcss";` in `app/globals.css` (plus the `@tailwindcss/postcss` PostCSS plugin the template configures). Then use utility classes: `className="flex gap-4 p-6 text-lg"`.

**Global CSS**: import a stylesheet in the root layout (`import './globals.css'`). Global styles apply to every route; keep them for resets, base typography and CSS variables. You can import global CSS from any component, but it still applies everywhere, so prefer the root layout.

**CSS Modules**: files named `*.module.css` are **locally scoped**. Import them as an object and use the generated class names: `import styles from './card.module.css'` then `className={styles.card}`. Class names are hashed, so they never collide across components. Sass is supported with the `sass` package (`.module.scss`).

CSS-in-JS libraries that need runtime JavaScript work only in Client Components and need extra setup; zero-runtime options and Tailwind fit Server Components best.

In production, CSS is automatically bundled, minified and code-split per route. Be aware that the order of CSS imports determines precedence when two rules conflict.
takeaways: Tailwind is the default; v4 needs only `@import "tailwindcss"` in globals.css
Import global CSS in the root layout; it applies to all routes
`*.module.css` gives locally scoped, hashed class names
pitfalls: Expecting a CSS Module class to apply when written as a plain string (`className="card"`); use `styles.card`.

quiz.q: What does importing styles from './button.module.css' give you?
options: Global CSS applied to every page
An object mapping your class names to unique, locally scoped class names
quiz.explain: CSS Modules generate unique class names so styles don't leak between components.

concepts.name: Optimised images and fonts
concepts.summary: Serve responsive, lazy-loaded images with next/image and self-hosted, layout-stable fonts with next/font.
concepts.why: Images and fonts are the biggest causes of slow loads and layout shift; Next.js fixes both with two components.
concepts.body: **`next/image`**'s `` component extends `` with automatic optimisation: - It serves resized, modern-format (WebP/AVIF) versions for each device size and lazy-loads by default. - It requires dimensions to prevent **layout shift**. Statically imported images (`import hero from './hero.jpg'`) provide `width`, `height` and a blur placeholder automatically. Remote images need explicit `width` and `height`, or `fill` to fill a positioned parent (with `sizes` describing the rendered width). - Remote hosts must be allowed in `next.config.ts` with `images.remotePatterns`. - For the hero image above the fold (your Largest Contentful Paint element), set `preload` so it loads early; the older `priority` prop is deprecated in Next.js 16. **`next/font`** downloads fonts at **build time** and self-hosts them with your app, so there are no requests to Google at runtime and no layout shift (it generates fallback metrics): ```tsx import { Inter } from 'next/font/google' const inter = Inter({ subsets: ['latin'] }) ``` Use `variable: '--font-inter'` to expose it as a CSS variable (handy with Tailwind). `next/font/local` loads font files from your project. Define fonts once in a shared module and reuse them; each call creates a separate font instance.
takeaways: `<Image>` resizes, converts and lazy-loads; dimensions prevent layout shift
Allow remote hosts with `images.remotePatterns`; use `preload` for the LCP image
`next/font` self-hosts fonts at build time with zero layout shift
pitfalls: Using a remote image URL without width/height (or fill) and without a matching remotePatterns entry, which fails.

quiz.q: When does next/font/google download the font files?
options: On every page request from the user's browser to Google
At build time; they are then served from your own domain
quiz.explain: next/font fetches and self-hosts fonts during the build, so no runtime requests go to Google.

concepts.name: Loading UI and streaming
concepts.summary: Show instant loading states with loading.tsx and Suspense, and stream slow parts of a page as they become ready.
concepts.why: Streaming keeps pages responsive when some data is slow, and loading boundaries make navigations feel instant.
concepts.body:
When a Server Component awaits slow data, nothing below it can render until the data arrives. **Streaming** splits the page into chunks so the server sends what's ready first and the rest as it resolves, over the same response.

Two ways to create streaming boundaries:

- **`loading.tsx`** in a route segment wraps that segment's page in a React `<Suspense>` boundary automatically. Its component shows immediately on navigation (the layout stays interactive) and is replaced by the page when it has rendered. It also makes navigations to dynamic routes feel instant, because the loading state can be prefetched.
- **`<Suspense fallback={...}>`** around individual components gives finer control: the static parts and other sections render immediately, and each suspended component streams in when its data is ready.

Design meaningful fallbacks: skeletons that match the final layout avoid jumps. Place boundaries around independent slow parts so they load in parallel rather than one blocking everything.

Streaming works with `use()` too: start a fetch in a Server Component without awaiting, pass the promise to a Client Component, and read it there inside Suspense.

Search engine bots that can't handle streaming get the fully rendered page instead; Next.js detects them. With Cache Components, Suspense boundaries also mark the request-time "holes" in a prerendered page, which you will learn next.
takeaways: `loading.tsx` wraps a segment's page in Suspense automatically
`<Suspense>` around slow components streams them independently
Separate boundaries let slow parts load in parallel without blocking the page
pitfalls: One Suspense boundary around the whole page, so the fastest content waits for the slowest.

quiz.q: A page has a heading and two slow components, each wrapped in its own Suspense boundary. What does the user see first?
options: A full-page spinner from loading.tsx always
The heading plus both fallbacks, then each component as its data arrives
quiz.explain: Content outside the boundaries is sent immediately and each boundary streams in independently.

concepts.name: Errors and not-found pages
concepts.summary: Handle expected errors as return values, uncaught errors with error.tsx boundaries, and missing resources with notFound().
concepts.why: Robust apps fail gracefully per section instead of showing a blank page or a generic crash.
concepts.body:
Next.js separates two kinds of errors.

**Expected errors** (validation failures, a 404 from an API) are part of normal operation. Model them as **return values**: render a message, or return an error object from a Server Action and show it with `useActionState`. Don't throw for these.

**Uncaught exceptions** are bugs or outages. Throw, and let an **error boundary** catch them:

- `error.tsx` in a segment wraps it in an error boundary. It must be a **Client Component** and receives `error` (the thrown value, typed `unknown`) and `retry`, which re-fetches and re-renders the segment. Errors bubble up to the nearest `error.tsx`, so the parent layout and navigation keep working.
- Errors from Server Components reach the client with the message stripped in production; use `error.digest` to match server logs.
- `global-error.tsx` handles errors in the root layout and must render its own `<html>` and `<body>`.
- `catchError` from `next/error` creates reusable component-level error boundaries.
- Error boundaries don't catch errors in event handlers; handle those with try/catch and state.

**Not found**: call `notFound()` from `next/navigation` when a resource doesn't exist. It renders the nearest `not-found.tsx` and sets a 404 status. `app/not-found.tsx` also handles unmatched URLs.
takeaways: Return expected errors as values; throw only for unexpected failures
`error.tsx` is a client error boundary per segment with `error` and `retry`
`notFound()` renders the nearest `not-found.tsx` with a 404 status
pitfalls: Writing `error.tsx` without `'use client'`, which fails because error boundaries need client-side React.

quiz.q: A widget in /dashboard/analytics throws during rendering and only app/dashboard/error.tsx exists. What does the user see?
options: The dashboard's error UI in place of the dashboard segment, with the root layout still working
quiz.explain: Errors bubble to the nearest error boundary, which replaces that segment while parents stay intact.

concepts.name: Server Actions and forms
concepts.summary: Mutate data with Server Functions: 'use server', form actions, useActionState for pending and error state, then revalidate or redirect.
concepts.why: Server Actions are the App Router's built-in way to handle forms and mutations without writing API routes.
concepts.body:
A **Server Function** is an async function marked with `'use server'` that runs on the server but can be called from the client. Used for mutations (forms, button clicks) it is called a **Server Action**.

Define them in a file starting with `'use server'` (all exports become actions), or inline inside a Server Component. Client Components can import actions from such a file but can't define them.

Pass an action to a form: `<form action={createTodo}>`. It receives the form's `FormData`. Forms with Server Actions work **before JavaScript loads** (progressive enhancement) and don't reload the page afterwards.

After mutating:

- `revalidatePath('/todos')` or tag-based revalidation refreshes cached data,
- `refresh()` from `next/cache` refreshes the current page's server data,
- `redirect('/todos/1')` navigates (it throws, so call it last).

For pending state and errors, use React's **`useActionState(action, initialState)`** in a Client Component. It returns `[state, formAction, pending]`; the action receives `(prevState, formData)` and returns the new state, e.g. `{ error: 'Title is required' }`.

Security: every Server Action is a **public POST endpoint**. Always validate input (e.g. with Zod) and check authentication and authorisation inside the action itself, just like an API route.
takeaways: `'use server'` functions run on the server and can be passed to `<form action>`
`useActionState` gives state, a wrapped action and a pending flag
After a mutation: revalidate, `refresh()` or `redirect()`
Every action is a public endpoint: validate input and check auth inside it
pitfalls: Relying on the UI hiding a button for authorisation; anyone can POST to the action directly.

quiz.q: Why must a Server Action check the user's permissions itself even if the button is only shown to admins?
options: Because actions run in the browser
Server Actions are reachable by direct POST requests, so UI visibility is not a security control
quiz.explain: Actions are exposed as POST endpoints; authorization must be enforced server-side in the action.

concepts.name: Route Handlers (API endpoints)
concepts.summary: Build HTTP endpoints with route.ts files using the Web Request and Response APIs.
concepts.why: Webhooks, public APIs, mobile backends and file downloads need real HTTP endpoints alongside your pages.
concepts.body:
A **Route Handler** is a `route.ts` file that exports functions named after HTTP methods: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`. It lives in `app/` like a page, for example `app/api/todos/route.ts` serves `/api/todos`. A folder can contain `page.tsx` or `route.ts`, not both.

Handlers use the standard Web APIs: they receive a `Request` (or `NextRequest`, which adds `nextUrl` and cookie helpers) and return a `Response`. `Response.json(data, { status: 201 })` is the common shortcut.

- Read JSON bodies with `await request.json()`, forms with `await request.formData()`, query params with `request.nextUrl.searchParams`.
- Dynamic segments work the same as for pages: the second argument has `params` as a Promise. Type it with the global `RouteContext<'/api/todos/[id]'>` helper.
- Use `cookies()` and `headers()` from `next/headers`, or read them from the request.

When should you use them? For your own UI, prefer Server Components for reads and Server Actions for mutations. Use Route Handlers for things that must be HTTP endpoints: webhooks from Stripe or GitHub, APIs consumed by mobile apps or third parties, OAuth callbacks, generated files, and streaming responses.

Like actions, they are public: authenticate and validate in every handler.
takeaways: `route.ts` exports GET/POST/... handlers using Web Request and Response
`params` arrive as a Promise in the second argument; type with `RouteContext`
Use them for webhooks and external APIs; prefer Server Components and Actions for your own UI
pitfalls: Fetching your own Route Handler from a Server Component; call the data function directly instead of making an HTTP round trip.

quiz.q: Your Server Component needs product data. A Route Handler at /api/products already returns it. What is the best approach?
options: Import and call the same data function the Route Handler uses, directly in the Server Component
Move the component to the client and fetch there
quiz.explain: Server Components can access data directly; an internal HTTP hop adds latency and complexity.

concepts.name: Metadata, SEO and OG images
concepts.summary: Set titles, descriptions and Open Graph data with the Metadata API, generate dynamic metadata, OG images, sitemaps and robots files.
concepts.why: Correct metadata decides how pages appear in search results and link previews.
concepts.body:
Next.js manages `<head>` through the **Metadata API**, only in Server Components (layouts and pages):

- **Static**: `export const metadata: Metadata = { title: 'About', description: '...' }`.
- **Dynamic**: `export async function generateMetadata({ params })` returns metadata based on data, e.g. a blog post's title. Fetches inside it are memoised with the page's identical requests.
- Metadata **merges** from the root layout down; a page overrides fields of its parents.
- **Title templates**: in a layout, `title: { template: '%s | Acme', default: 'Acme' }` turns a page's `title: 'Pricing'` into "Pricing | Acme".
- `openGraph`, `twitter`, `alternates.canonical`, `robots` and `icons` cover social previews and SEO. Set `metadataBase` in the root layout so relative URLs resolve to absolute ones.

**File conventions** generate assets and routes:

- `opengraph-image.tsx` (or `.png`) creates the social preview image; dynamic ones use `ImageResponse` from `next/og` to render JSX to a PNG.
- `icon.png`, `apple-icon.png`, `favicon.ico` in `app/` become icons.
- `sitemap.ts` and `robots.ts` export functions returning typed objects (`MetadataRoute.Sitemap`, `MetadataRoute.Robots`) that become `/sitemap.xml` and `/robots.txt`.

Use `generateViewport` or `export const viewport` for viewport and theme colour settings.
takeaways: Export `metadata` or `generateMetadata` from layouts and pages (server only)
Metadata merges top-down; title templates add a site suffix
`opengraph-image`, `icon`, `sitemap.ts`, `robots.ts` are file conventions
pitfalls: Adding `<title>` tags manually in components or exporting metadata from a Client Component; use the Metadata API in server files.

quiz.q: The root layout sets title: { template: '%s | Acme', default: 'Acme' } and a page sets title: 'Pricing'. What is the document title?
quiz.explain: The page's title is inserted into the parent's template.

concepts.name: Environment variables and configuration
concepts.summary: Load secrets and settings from .env files, expose only NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables to the browser, and configure next.config.ts.
concepts.why: Leaking a secret into the client bundle is one of the most common and costly Next.js mistakes.
concepts.body:
Next.js loads environment variables from `.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.development`, `.env.production` (and `.test` variants), in a defined precedence order where `.env.local` overrides `.env`. Commit `.env` defaults if useful, never `.env.local` with secrets.

The crucial rule: variables are **server-only by default**. `process.env.DATABASE_URL` works in Server Components, Server Actions and Route Handlers but is `undefined` in the browser. Only variables prefixed with **`NEXT_PUBLIC_`** are exposed to client code, and they are **inlined at build time** into the JavaScript bundle. So a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` value can't change after building without rebuilding, and anything prefixed is public.

To keep server code from being imported into Client Components by accident, add `import 'server-only'` at the top of modules that use secrets; importing them from client code fails the build.

**`next.config.ts`** configures the framework with a typed `NextConfig` object. Commonly used options:

- `images.remotePatterns` for remote images,
- `redirects()` and `rewrites()` for URL rules,
- `headers()` for security headers,
- `output: 'standalone'` for container deployments,
- `cacheComponents`, `reactCompiler`, `typedRoutes` and experimental flags.

Validate required environment variables at startup (for example with Zod) so misconfiguration fails fast.
takeaways: Env vars are server-only unless prefixed with `NEXT_PUBLIC_`
`NEXT_PUBLIC_` values are inlined at build time and visible to everyone
`import 'server-only'` guards secret-using modules; `next.config.ts` holds framework settings
pitfalls: Prefixing a secret API key with `NEXT_PUBLIC_` to make it work in a client component, publishing it in the bundle.

quiz.q: A Client Component reads process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY. What value does it get in the browser?
options: undefined, because only NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are exposed to the client
An empty string after a warning
quiz.explain: Unprefixed variables are only available on the server.

concepts.name: Prerendering and the static shell
concepts.summary: Understand what Next.js prerenders at build time, what must wait for a request, and how Suspense, connection() and generateStaticParams shape the static shell.
concepts.why: With Cache Components, every route is a mix of prerendered and request-time parts; placing them well decides speed.
concepts.body:
With **Cache Components** (on by default in new apps), Next.js renders each route at build time and keeps whatever can complete as a **static shell**: HTML plus an RSC payload that can be served instantly from a CDN. Parts that need request data are left as **holes** that stream in at request time. This is called **Partial Prerendering**.

What can be prerendered:

- static markup, module imports and pure computation,
- results of `'use cache'` functions and components (next lessons).

What can't, and must be wrapped in `<Suspense>` so the rest of the page can still prerender:

- **runtime APIs**: `cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams`, and `params` that aren't known at build time,
- **uncached data**: fetches and database queries without `'use cache'`,
- **per-request values** like `Date.now()` or `crypto.randomUUID()`, which require `await connection()` first.

If such access isn't inside a Suspense boundary, the dev overlay reports a **blocking route** and suggests the fix. The deeper in the tree you await, the more of the page lands in the shell: pass the `params` promise down instead of awaiting it in a layout.

**`generateStaticParams`** returns the param values to prerender at build time, e.g. your 100 most popular product slugs. Other values render the shell immediately and fill in on demand.

Apps without Cache Components use the previous model, where any runtime API makes the whole route dynamic.
takeaways: Each route = prerendered static shell + Suspense holes filled at request time
Runtime APIs, uncached data and per-request values must sit inside `<Suspense>`
`generateStaticParams` prerenders known dynamic params; `connection()` defers to request time
pitfalls: Reading `cookies()` at the top of a layout, which pushes everything below it out of the static shell.

quiz.q: With Cache Components, a page reads cookies() in one small component. How do you keep the rest of the page prerendered?
options: Move cookies() into the root layout
You can't; any cookie read makes the page dynamic
Wrap that component in <Suspense> so only it renders at request time
quiz.explain: Suspense marks the runtime access as a hole; everything outside it stays in the static shell.

concepts.name: Caching with 'use cache'
concepts.summary: Cache functions, components and pages with the use cache directive, control lifetimes with cacheLife and label entries with cacheTag.
concepts.why: Explicit caching is how Next.js 16 apps get static speed for data that changes rarely, without stale-data surprises.
concepts.body:
The **`'use cache'`** directive caches the return value of an async function, component or whole page. Put it at the top of the function body (or the top of a file to cache all its exports).

- **Data level**: `async function getProducts() { 'use cache'; ... }` shares the result wherever it's used.
- **UI level**: a cached Server Component or page caches its rendered output.

The **cache key** is built automatically from the function's identity, its **arguments** and any values it **captures** from outer scopes, so `getProduct('a')` and `getProduct('b')` are separate entries. Arguments and return values must be serialisable. You can't call `cookies()` or `headers()` inside a cached scope; read them outside and pass the values in as arguments.

**`cacheLife(profile)`** sets the lifetime. Built-in profiles are `seconds`, `minutes`, `hours`, `days`, `weeks` and `max` (or a custom `{ stale, revalidate, expire }` object). Without it the `default` profile applies (stale 5 min, revalidate 15 min). Very short lifetimes are treated as request-time holes rather than baked into the static shell.

**`cacheTag('products')`** labels entries so you can invalidate them on demand.

Variants: `'use cache: remote'` stores entries in a shared, durable cache handler (the default store is in-memory per instance), and `'use cache: private'` caches per user data that reads cookies, only in the browser.
takeaways: `'use cache'` caches a function, component or page; arguments and captured values form the key
`cacheLife` sets stale/revalidate/expire; `cacheTag` labels entries for invalidation
Read cookies/headers outside and pass values in; `use cache: remote` / `private` are variants
pitfalls: Calling `cookies()` inside a `'use cache'` function; runtime APIs aren't allowed in cached scopes.

quiz.q: getUser(id) uses 'use cache'. It is called with id 1 and then id 2. How many cache entries exist?
options: One, keyed by the function name
Two, because arguments are part of the cache key
One per page that calls it
quiz.explain: The cache key includes serialised arguments, so different ids produce different entries.

concepts.name: Revalidating cached data
concepts.summary: Keep cached data fresh with time-based lifetimes and on-demand invalidation: revalidateTag, updateTag, revalidatePath and refresh.
concepts.why: Caching is only safe if you can update it the moment data changes.
concepts.body:
Cached data needs a way to become fresh again. Next.js offers two strategies.

**Time-based**: the `cacheLife` profile decides when entries go stale and are regenerated in the background (stale-while-revalidate), and when they expire completely.

**On-demand**, after a mutation:

- **`updateTag(tag)`** expires tagged entries immediately so the user who made the change sees it on the next render (read-your-own-writes). It can only be called in **Server Actions**.
- **`revalidateTag(tag, profile)`** marks entries stale with stale-while-revalidate semantics: visitors may get the old version once while a fresh one is generated. In Next.js 16 the second argument is required; `'max'` is recommended. Usable in Server Actions and Route Handlers, e.g. a CMS webhook.
- **`revalidatePath('/blog')`** invalidates everything for a path (add `'layout'` to include nested routes). Simple, but coarser than tags.
- **`refresh()`** re-renders the current page's uncached server data from a Server Action; it doesn't touch tagged caches.

Choosing: user edits their own profile, use `updateTag` in the action. Editor publishes in a CMS, the webhook route calls `revalidateTag('posts', 'max')`. Tag precisely (`post:42` as well as `posts`) so you can invalidate narrowly.

All caches are scoped to one deployment: a new deploy starts with fresh prerenders.
takeaways: `cacheLife` handles time-based freshness
`updateTag` (Server Actions only) for read-your-own-writes; `revalidateTag(tag, 'max')` for background refresh
`revalidatePath` invalidates by route; `refresh()` re-renders uncached data
pitfalls: Calling `revalidateTag('posts')` without the second argument, which Next.js 16 requires.

quiz.q: A user edits their profile in a Server Action and must see the change immediately. Which call fits best?
quiz.explain: updateTag expires the entries immediately for read-your-own-writes; revalidateTag may serve stale content once.

concepts.name: Proxy (formerly Middleware)
concepts.summary: Run code before requests complete with proxy.ts: redirects, rewrites, headers and lightweight auth checks, scoped with matchers.
concepts.why: Request-level logic such as locale redirects, A/B tests and optimistic auth gates belongs in Proxy.
concepts.body:
**Proxy** runs before a request reaches your routes. Since Next.js 16, the feature formerly called Middleware is named Proxy: create `proxy.ts` in the project root (or `src/`) and export a function named `proxy` (or a default export). Only one Proxy file is supported, but it can import modules.

The function receives a `NextRequest` and can:

- `NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/login', request.url))`,
- `NextResponse.rewrite(url)` to serve a different route while keeping the URL (A/B tests, multi-tenant hosts),
- `NextResponse.next()` to continue, optionally setting request or response headers and cookies,
- return a `Response` directly.

Limit where it runs with `export const config = { matcher: [...] }`. Exclude static assets and images, or every file request pays the cost.

Proxy uses the **Node.js runtime** by default in Next.js 16 (the `runtime` option isn't allowed in Proxy files). Keep it fast: it runs on every matched request.

Good uses: redirects based on cookies or headers, locale detection, rewrites, adding security headers, and **optimistic auth checks** (is there a session cookie at all?). Not good: slow data fetching or being your only authorisation layer. Verify sessions again close to the data, in the data access layer or each action. For static redirects, prefer `redirects()` in `next.config.ts`.
takeaways: `proxy.ts` (formerly `middleware.ts`) runs before matched requests
Redirect, rewrite, set headers or respond; scope it with `config.matcher`
Runs on Node.js by default; keep it fast and use it for optimistic checks only
pitfalls: Doing the only authorisation check in Proxy; Server Actions and Route Handlers must verify access themselves.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between NextResponse.rewrite and NextResponse.redirect?
options: rewrite serves another route while the browser URL stays the same; redirect tells the browser to go to a new URL
redirect works only for external URLs
rewrite changes the URL but not the content
quiz.explain: A rewrite is internal; a redirect sends a 3xx response and the URL in the browser changes.

concepts.name: Route groups, parallel and intercepting routes
concepts.summary: Organise routes with (groups), render several pages at once with @slots, and build URL-backed modals with intercepting routes.
concepts.why: Dashboards, modals and multiple root layouts need routing patterns beyond simple folders.
concepts.body:
**Route groups**: a folder in parentheses, like `(marketing)`, organises routes without affecting the URL. `app/(marketing)/about/page.tsx` is `/about`. Groups let different sections have different layouts, and even **multiple root layouts** (each group with its own `layout.tsx` containing `<html>`).

**Private folders**: `_lib` or `_components` are excluded from routing entirely.

**Parallel routes** render several pages in the same layout simultaneously. Named **slots** are folders starting with `@`: `app/dashboard/@team/page.tsx` and `@analytics/page.tsx` are passed to `app/dashboard/layout.tsx` as `team` and `analytics` props next to `children`. Each slot has its own loading and error states and can be shown conditionally (e.g. based on the user's role). Add `default.tsx` to a slot as the fallback when the slot has no match for the current URL after a full page load; otherwise you get a 404.

**Intercepting routes** load a route inside the current layout during client navigation, while a direct visit shows the full page. The convention mirrors relative paths: `(.)photo` intercepts a sibling segment, `(..)` one level up, `(...)` from the root. Combined with a parallel `@modal` slot, this creates a **URL-backed modal**: clicking a photo opens a modal with a shareable URL; refreshing shows the photo page; back closes it.

**`template.tsx`** is like a layout but remounts on every navigation, for enter animations or per-page effects.
takeaways: `(group)` folders organise routes and layouts without changing URLs
`@slot` folders are parallel routes passed to the layout as props; add `default.tsx`
`(.)`, `(..)`, `(...)` intercept routes for URL-backed modals
pitfalls: Forgetting `default.tsx` in a parallel slot, so a hard refresh of another URL renders a 404.

quiz.q: With @modal/(.)photos/[id] and photos/[id], what does a user see when opening /photos/7 directly in a new tab?
options: The modal over the previous page
The full photos/[id] page, because interception only applies to client-side navigation
quiz.explain: Intercepting routes take effect on soft navigation; direct loads render the real route.

concepts.name: Authentication and data security
concepts.summary: Secure a Next.js app: sessions in cookies, a server-only Data Access Layer, authorisation in every action and handler, and safe data passed to clients.
concepts.why: The App Router blurs the client-server line, so security mistakes leak data or expose mutations easily.
concepts.body:
Auth in Next.js is usually built with a library (Auth.js, Clerk, Better Auth and others) or your own **session cookie**: an encrypted or signed, `httpOnly`, `secure`, `sameSite` cookie set in a Server Action at login and read with `cookies()`.

Where to check access:

- **Data Access Layer (DAL)**: a `server-only` module that verifies the session and exposes functions like `getCurrentUser()` and `getInvoices()`. Wrap the session check in React's `cache()` so it runs once per request. Every read of protected data goes through it.
- **Server Actions and Route Handlers**: verify authentication and authorisation inside each one; they are public endpoints.
- **Proxy**: only optimistic redirects (no cookie, go to login), never the sole check.
- **Layouts aren't a security boundary**: they may not re-render on navigation, so check in pages or the DAL, close to the data.

Data exposure:

- Return **DTOs**: only the fields the UI needs, not whole database rows with password hashes.
- Remember that props passed to Client Components are sent to the browser.
- React's experimental **taint** APIs (enabled with the `taint` config option) can block specific objects or values from ever crossing to the client.

Also validate all input with a schema library, rate-limit sensitive actions, and treat `searchParams` and `params` as untrusted.
takeaways: Centralise session checks in a `server-only` Data Access Layer, cached per request
Authorise inside every Server Action and Route Handler; Proxy is optimistic only
Return minimal DTOs; everything passed to Client Components is public
pitfalls: Checking auth only in a layout, assuming it protects all child pages and their data.

quiz.q: Why is checking authentication only in a shared layout insufficient?
options: Layouts may not re-render on navigation and don't protect the data functions, actions or route handlers
Layouts run only on the client
quiz.explain: Security checks belong close to the data: in the DAL, pages, actions and handlers.

concepts.name: Caching without Cache Components
concepts.summary: Read and maintain apps on the previous caching model: fetch cache options, route segment config, unstable_cache and static vs dynamic routes.
concepts.why: Most existing Next.js 13 to 15 apps use this model, and you will maintain or migrate them.
concepts.body:
Apps that don't enable `cacheComponents` use the **previous model**, which you will meet in most existing codebases.

**Routes are static or dynamic as a whole.** At build time Next.js tries to prerender each route. Using a runtime API (`cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams`, `connection()`) or an uncached `fetch` marked `cache: 'no-store'` makes the entire route **dynamic**, rendered per request. Otherwise it is static, even if it fetched data at build time.

**Caching is configured per request or per route:**

- `fetch(url, { cache: 'force-cache' })` caches a request; since Next.js 15 the default is not cached.
- `fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 3600, tags: ['posts'] } })` caches with a lifetime and tags.
- `unstable_cache(fn, keyParts, { revalidate, tags })` caches non-fetch work like database queries.
- **Route segment config** exports in a page or layout: `export const revalidate = 60` (ISR: regenerate at most every 60 s), `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` or `'force-static'`, `dynamicParams`, `fetchCache`.

On-demand invalidation uses the same `revalidatePath` and `revalidateTag(tag, profile)` functions.

These segment options are **removed** when Cache Components is enabled. Migrating means replacing `revalidate` exports and fetch options with `'use cache'` + `cacheLife`, and wrapping runtime access in Suspense. The official migration guide walks through it.
takeaways: Previous model: a route is entirely static or dynamic
Cache via fetch options, `unstable_cache` and segment config like `revalidate`
These options are removed under Cache Components; migrate to `'use cache'` + `cacheLife`
pitfalls: Copying `export const revalidate` into an app with Cache Components enabled, where it is no longer allowed.

quiz.q: In the previous model, a page reads cookies() in one small component. What happens to the route?
options: cookies() returns empty at build time and the page stays static
Only that component renders per request
The whole route becomes dynamic and renders on every request
quiz.explain: Without Cache Components, runtime APIs opt the entire route into dynamic rendering.

concepts.name: RSC payload, prefetching and the client cache
concepts.summary: Understand what actually travels over the wire: the RSC payload, how the router prefetches and caches segments, and what makes navigations instant or slow.
concepts.why: Diagnosing slow navigations, stale UI and excessive server load requires knowing how the App Router works under the hood.
concepts.body:
A Next.js page is rendered on the server into the **RSC payload** (React's Flight format): the output of Server Components, placeholders and chunk references for Client Components, and the serialised props passed to them. On a first visit the server also turns it into HTML; the browser shows the HTML, then React uses the payload to reconcile and hydrate Client Components.

On **client navigations** no HTML is fetched: the router requests the RSC payload for the changed segments only and merges it into the current tree, so shared layouts keep their state. A **Server Action** response carries both the action's return value and, if it revalidated data, a fresh payload for the current route in one round trip.

**Prefetching**: `<Link>` prefetches routes as they enter the viewport or on hover. With Partial Prefetching (the default in new apps), the router prefetches each route's **App Shell** (static content plus session data); `prefetch={true}` additionally renders cached, URL-dependent content per link at the cost of a server invocation each. Prefetched payloads live in the **client cache** for their `stale` lifetime (from `cacheLife`, or `staleTimes` config).

What makes navigation slow: dynamic routes without a `loading.tsx` or Suspense boundary (nothing can show until the server responds), dynamic params not covered by `generateStaticParams`, large payloads (props passed to Client Components are serialised into every payload) and slow networks. `useLinkStatus()` can show pending state on the clicked link.
takeaways: Server Components render to an RSC payload; HTML is only for the first load
Navigations fetch payloads for changed segments and merge them into the tree
Link prefetches App Shells into a client cache with a stale lifetime
Missing loading boundaries and large serialised props make navigations slow
pitfalls: Passing large objects to Client Components, bloating every RSC payload and HTML response.

quiz.q: During a client-side navigation between two pages that share a layout, what does the browser request?
options: The RSC payload for the segments that changed
Nothing; everything is precomputed in the bundle
The full HTML of the new page
quiz.explain: Soft navigations fetch RSC payloads for changed segments; shared layouts are reused.

quiz.q: A dynamic route has no loading.tsx and no Suspense boundaries. Why can navigation to it feel unresponsive?
options: It triggers a full page reload
Link doesn't work with dynamic routes
Nothing can be shown until the server finishes rendering, so the click appears to do nothing
quiz.explain: Without a loading boundary there is no prefetchable fallback, so the UI waits for the full server response.

concepts.name: How Server Actions work
concepts.summary: Know the mechanics behind Server Actions: action IDs, POST requests, closure encryption, sequential dispatch, limits and deployment skew.
concepts.why: Understanding the wire protocol prevents security holes, performance traps and production errors after deploys.
concepts.body:
At build time the `'use server'` directive makes the compiler replace a Server Function in client bundles with a **reference**: an **encrypted, non-deterministic action ID**. Calling it sends a **POST request** to the current page with the ID and serialised arguments; the server looks the function up, runs it and streams back the result (and possibly a fresh RSC payload). Only POST can invoke actions.

Built-in protections:

- **CSRF**: the `Origin` header must match the host; configure `serverActions.allowedOrigins` behind proxies.
- **Body size** is capped at 1 MB by default (`serverActions.bodySizeLimit`).
- **Dead code elimination**: actions not referenced by client code have no public endpoint.
- **Closures**: values captured by an inline action (like an `id` from the page) are **encrypted** and sent to the client and back. Don't rely on that for secrets; pass only references (ids) and re-read data on the server. In multi-instance deployments set a stable `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.

Behaviour to design around:

- The client **dispatches actions one at a time**; `Promise.all` over several actions won't parallelise them. Do parallel work inside one action, or use Route Handlers for non-mutating requests.
- Actions are for mutations, not data fetching.
- New deployments generate new IDs; a tab still running the old build gets "Failed to find Server Action". Prefer rolling deploys and offer a refresh.
takeaways: Actions compile to encrypted IDs invoked by POST to the current page
CSRF origin check, 1 MB body limit and dead code elimination are built in
Captured closure values are encrypted but must still be treated as untrusted
Clients dispatch actions sequentially; deploys rotate action IDs
pitfalls: Using `Promise.all` to run several Server Actions in parallel from the client; they are dispatched one after another.

quiz.q: A client calls three Server Actions with Promise.all. How are they executed?
options: The client dispatches them one at a time, each waiting for the previous
quiz.explain: Next.js dispatches Server Actions sequentially per client to keep the re-rendered tree consistent.

concepts.name: Deployment, runtimes and self-hosting
concepts.summary: Deploy Next.js to Vercel, a Node.js server, containers or static hosting, and understand runtimes, cache handlers, after() and version skew.
concepts.why: Production behaviour (caching, scaling, streaming) depends on how and where the app is deployed.
concepts.body:
Deployment targets:

- **Node.js server**: `next build` then `next start`. All features work. Put a reverse proxy (such as nginx) in front for TLS, compression and slow-client protection.
- **Docker**: set `output: 'standalone'` so the build produces a minimal server (`.next/standalone/server.js`) with only the needed `node_modules`; copy `public/` and `.next/static` next to it.
- **Static export**: `output: 'export'` writes plain HTML/JS to `out/` for any static host, but drops server features (actions, runtime rendering, image optimisation by default, Proxy).
- **Platforms**: Vercel supports everything natively; other platforms integrate through **deployment adapters**.

**Runtime**: pages, Route Handlers and Proxy run on Node.js. The older **Edge runtime** (`export const runtime = 'edge'`) is deprecated, and with Cache Components the `runtime` export isn't supported at all, so remove it when you meet it in older code.

**Caching across instances**: prerendered HTML lives on disk and `'use cache'` entries in memory per instance. With several instances, configure a shared **cache handler** (`cacheHandlers` config, `'use cache: remote'`) and a stable **deployment ID** and `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.

**`after(fn)`** from `next/server` runs work after the response is sent (logging, analytics) without delaying users.

**Version skew**: clients on an old build may request assets or actions from a new one; a consistent `deploymentId` lets Next.js detect this and hard-reload.
concepts.code:
# Dockerfile (standalone output)
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build                     # next.config.ts has output: 'standalone'

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000
COPY --from=build /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=build /app/.next/static ./.next/static
COPY --from=build /app/public ./public
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# app/api/checkout/route.ts - log after responding
# import { after } from 'next/server'
# export async function POST(req: Request) {
#   const order = await createOrder(await req.json())
#   after(() => analytics.track('order', { id: order.id }))   // runs after the response
#   return Response.json(order, { status: 201 })
# }
takeaways: `next start` on Node.js supports everything; `output: 'standalone'` suits containers
`output: 'export'` produces static files but drops server features
Multi-instance setups need a shared cache handler, deployment ID and stable action key
`after()` runs non-critical work after the response
pitfalls: Running several self-hosted instances with the default in-memory cache and per-build keys, causing inconsistent caches and failed actions.

quiz.q: Which config makes next build produce a minimal server.js with only the required node_modules for Docker?
quiz.explain: Standalone output traces dependencies and emits a self-contained server for containers.
